title: Here's how Democrats in Congress are preparing for election fraud claims
description: Voters are already casting votes in aa n
body:
Voters are already casting votes in aa number of states ahead of the midterm election on Nov. 3.
                
                    RYAN MURPHY/AFP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        RYAN MURPHY/AFP
    

   
   This story has been updated from a story first reported in August.   This midterm cycle, the Trump administration has gathered millions of state voter records for law enforcement purposes, endeavored to restrict mail-in voting nationwide, declined the typical practice of inviting international election observers and repeatedly raised the idea of dispatching armed federal personnel to  voting locations.   The Trump administration broadly describes its actions as an effort to ensure the integrity of the American democratic system after the president's signature election overhaul effort, the SAVE America Act, foundered in the GOP-led Senate.   In a statement to NPR in October, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said that "President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections. While extreme Democrats and the media continue to dismiss concerns about voter fraud, the Trump Administration is taking decisive action to protect our elections including prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion."   
   This summer, NPR spoke to more than a dozen people who've formed what they describe as an election protection task force. It's a coordinated effort between Democratic lawmakers and their staffers, election litigators, scholars and nonpartisan good governance organizations.   Those involved worry that the administration will point to normal, but poorly understood, parts of American election infrastructure, including slow vote counting in California and Alaska, as evidence of fraudulent behavior. They also say that the administration has long worked to undermine public trust in a secure and transparent election system and has, without constitutional authority, inserted the executive branch into the state-led election process.   Democracy Forward — a legal nonprofit that says it works to advance democracy and social progress through litigation, policy and public education — has written that the Trump administration's efforts "harness the president's longstanding and baseless conspiracy theories in pursuit of discovering so-called 'election fraud.' These actions are reckless and run the risk of intimidating and disenfranchising voters."   Even as task force members acknowledged there is no magic "protect democracy" button tucked away in a Capitol cloakroom, they each emphasized the power of legislators as messengers and organizers. Their primary goal is to to prepare the public and their state and local counterparts to act when necessary to ensure election results are honored.   
   Establishing the midterm narrative   "We have very important elections coming up," Trump said in a July address from the East Room of the White House. "We want those elections to be honest."   He used the speech to call on Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would, among other measures, require voters to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote and a photo ID before they can cast a ballot.   "How easy is that to do, unless you want to cheat? The only reason you wouldn't do it is you want to cheat because your policies are so bad, and your candidates are so pathetic that you can't get away or can't get elected any other way," he said.   Members of the Democratic task force said the remarks should be understood as an effort to make voter fraud — which studies and investigations have found to be vanishingly rare — seem plausible.   Justin Vail, a leader at Protect Democracy, a cross-ideological group that says it uses litigation, advocacy and research to protect American elections is a member of the task force. He previously served as a special assistant to President Joe Biden, working on democracy issues. He told NPR that Trump's speech was an effort to sow doubt in November's elections, a first step in what his organization characterizes as a three-step playbook: deceive, disrupt and deny.   "First, he deceives Americans, manufacturing false claims about voter fraud and the security of our elections," Vail said. "Second, he seeks to disrupt the normal state and local management of elections," he continued, "in an attempt to coerce them to enact policies that threaten the eligible voters' access. And if that's all not enough, Trump is prepared to outright deny election results that he doesn't like."   The fight in courts   Marc Elias, the prominent election litigator and a member of the task force, describes the election protection effort on a continuum.   
   "It begins with voter registration, then you have people voting, then you have Election Day," Elias said. "You have tabulation of ballots, you have local certification, and ultimately you have seating."   "History has shown that Donald Trump is willing to weaponize power against all points of that process," Elias said. "This is not something that we wait until election subversion has taken place."   Elias' firm has been at the leading edge of election-related litigation against the administration. He said his team has been combating what he views as the first stage of an ongoing election interference effort. They have been involved in dozens of lawsuits spanning every state.   A primary fight centered on mail-in ballots. Trump ordered the Postal Service to deliver mail-in ballots only to registered voters on those lists — an effort that was ultimately halted by the Supreme Court.   The Department of Homeland Security has also worked for months to gather state voter rolls, which it says it is using to find noncitizens who are illegally registered to vote.   A tally by the State Democracy Research Initiative at the University of Wisconsin-Madison has tallied 31 federal lawsuits from the administration seeking state voter data. States have largely refused to comply, citing privacy laws and the Constitution, which expressly delegates election administration to the states subject to congressional oversight.   Common Cause, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization, challenged the Justice Department's voter data collection program as violating federal law in court. On October 9, 2026, a federal district court ruled that the policy exceeds the Justice Department's authority, is arbitrary and capricious, and violates federal law.   The court vacated the policy nationwide, impacting not only the Justice Department's efforts to get data from the states that have resisted as well as states that had already voluntarily complied. The Justice Department has appealed the decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.   
   The limits of Congress   Limited in their ability to exercise hard power, Democratic lawmakers have exercised power in other ways. Primarily, elected Democrats are focused on being the connective tissue between their state and local counterparts involved in the mechanics of administering elections and the good governance groups involved in ensuring the integrity of that process.   "We recognize that elections are run at the local level, at the state level, and we want to be able to partner — and continue to partner — with our state authorities as they carry out their duties," said Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, D-Del., told NPR in August.   "But we also know that, especially at this moment, there are civil society organizations, there are attorneys, there are community leaders who are all coming together and saying we're each going to do our part to ensure that this election is safe, reliable, strong, that workers at the polls are protected, that our voters can get out there and vote," she said.   Still, Elias believes Congress could play a larger role in protecting elections if it was able to speak with a unified, bipartisan voice, but "it's not doing that because Mike Johnson and John Thune aren't doing it," he said, referring to the top Republicans in the House and Senate, respectively.   "Imagine," Elias said, "a brief that was submitted by the House of Representatives itself, the U.S. Senate itself, telling the courts that Congress was jealously guarding its authority" over elections. "That, I think, would frankly be an incredibly useful thing and would have a real impact."   GOP legislators broadly echo the president's election fraud narratives, and leaders have shown little desire to push back on his election-related actions. Congressional Republicans have instead focused much of their attention on trying to pass the SAVE America Act.   
   Despite their minority status, Democrats do have access to some oversight tools. While the House of Representatives has an active staff election observer program that dates to the 1980s, this year will see the first-ever Senate election observer program.   Staff designated by lawmakers of both parties can be dispatched to observe voting and tabulating locations, with the goal of keeping lawmakers informed for oversight work and in case of contested results. Those who volunteer to participate will not advocate for candidates, participate in vote counting or interfere with voters or election staff.   "I am committed to using every tool to protect free and fair elections, and the new Senate Election Observer Program will do just that," Padilla, the top Democrat on the Senate committee that oversees election administration, said in a statement announcing the program.   Senate Democratic Majority Leader Schumer and Padilla announced this month that more than 100 staff had agreed to participate. Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., who chairs the committee, has not addressed whether Republican staffers would participate.   What comes next   Some members of the task force are now prepared for worst-case scenarios with prewritten legal briefs and a Rolodex of key contacts in places they believe to be high risk. Their lists include areas in which election officials may have echoed the president's election denial rhetoric, where results are expected to be close or slow to count, and where Trump has focused scrutiny in the past, like California, Illinois and New York.   Several members noted that over the last year, Trump has attempted to dramatically expand direct federal involvement in elections and asserted unprecedented authority over election administration.   "Remember, the States are merely an 'agent' for the Federal Government in counting and tabulating the votes," he wrote on Truth Social last August. "They must do what the Federal Government, as represented by the President of the United States, tells them, FOR THE GOOD OF OUR COUNTRY, to do."   
   Multiple election law experts consulted for this story, none of whom are involved in advising congressional lawmakers or candidates, broadly agreed that the president has no role in election administration, which the Constitution delegates explicitly to the states and Congress.   Despite the risks they see, many of those involved in congressional Democrats' election preparations felt optimistic that, in the end, the voice of the American public would win out.   Vanita Gupta, formerly Biden's associate attorney general and now director of the Center for Law and Public Trust at New York University's law school, is among those optimistic voices.   "Hundreds of nonpartisan organizations have been preparing over the past year to do everything in our power to protect the integrity of our elections," Gupta told NPR in August. "Maybe the process of getting from here to a new Congress may be messier than any of us would like, perhaps filled with a lot more litigation and organizing than we might have thought was necessary, but we are going to have free and fair elections so long as people don't take for granted their right to vote."

title: Senate candidates built up massive campaign war chests with out-of-state donations
description: Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaks during a
body:
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaks during a campaign event on October 17, 2026 in Marietta, Georgia.
                
                    Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images
    

   
   📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App      In key U.S. Senate races this year, candidates are soliciting donations from outside of their home states, and their out-of-state messaging is different from what they're running locally.   An NPR analysis of Google Ads for four major Senate races — Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas — found that the Democratic and Republican candidates spent more than $15 million on advertising related to fundraising in the 2025-26 election cycle. About three quarters of that went to ads that ran nationally.   
    Loading... 
   Often, these ads focus on national talking points — such as attacking or defending President Trump, or turning the Senate blue or red — rather than local issues. For candidates like Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Iowa Democratic nominee Josh Turek, more than 80% of their itemized individual contributions have come from out of state.    Loading... 
   The funneling of funds has affected at least four of the competitive Senate races, where a majority of the money is coming from outside the state. ActBlue and WinRed, two major grassroots fundraising platforms, are a major catalyst for out-of-state fundraising.   Because this technology is inexpensive to run, it incentivizes candidates to rely on digital ads, according to Zachary Albert, a professor of politics at Brandeis University.   "ActBlue and WinRed really reduced the transaction costs for contributing," Albert said. "Even if you're only yielding like a $5 or $10 contribution from someone like the costs of soliciting that are so much lower than they used to be, that it makes it worthwhile."   With both parties — and each candidate — now having fundraising platforms, political hopefuls increasingly need to stand out from the crowd and are often shifting their messaging to a broader audience, which can result in using polarizing messaging to solicit funds.   Nationalized talking points   For in-state and out-of-state ads, candidates tend to have two different sets of talking points, according to Wesleyan Media Project's Michael Franz.   
   "In a general election campaign for a [local] TV ad, a candidate will never say, 'I'm the Democrat,' because they want to appeal to moderates and swing voters and they want voters across the aisle," Franz said. "But with a digital ad that's airing outside of your state, the party label becomes more important."    This is reflected in many digital ads. Former Ohio Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown — who is seeking to regain a place in the Senate — calls to turn his state blue while Georgia Republican Rep. Mike Collins asks people to help turn his state's Senate seat red. Republicans currently control the Senate but there are a number of toss-up races giving Democrats a path to taking back the chamber.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Iowa Republican Senate candidate, Rep. Ashley Hinson speaks at a rally on October 22, 2026 in Sioux City, Iowa as President Trump looks on.
                
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
    

   
   Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson touts her America First credentials in ads for her Senate race, saying she's "America First," while Ossoff in Georgia attacks Trump directly.   According to Michael Heseltine, a researcher at Oxford University who studies how members of congress use social media to communicate, says while there is a large amount of locally-focused messaging, candidates are increasingly spending more time and energy on national talking points.   "[If] we continue on that trend, you'll probably find more and more members who have neglected their constituencies or at least not presented themselves as representatives of their constituencies," he said.   In a statement to NPR, the Ossoff campaign denied targeting audiences by location, and says the campaign "is powered by small-dollar donors because the Senator refuses donations from corporate PACs and federal lobbyists."   The other campaigns declined to comment or did not respond to interview requests.   Daniel Hopkins, a political science professor at the University of Pennsylvania, believes we're in a new era of campaigning, where candidates now have two major stakeholders to appeal to: a voter base which is local, and a donor base which is often larger and nationwide.   
   "When Jon Ossoff is trying to compete for votes, he's competing against Georgia Republicans," Hopkins said. "But when Jon Ossoff is trying to compete for dollars, he's competing for attention and for donations, ultimately with other prominent Democratic candidates."   The rise of out of state funds   The amount of out-of-state funds for congressional campaigns has been rising each election cycle, according to OpenSecrets.   In order to get these funds, candidates are urged to promote the party platform. Hopkins attributes this to two causes; the party platforms becoming more homogenous and changes in campaign finance laws.    
   "It used to be that the pathway to success was to rise up through your local party, building the support of local elites in your community," he said.   "The path to political success increasingly goes through a set of, 'ATM districts' around the country that are known to give a lot of money either to Democrats or the Republicans," Hopkins explained.   In states that are dominated by one party, donors might elect to send their funds to a more competitive state to help influence elections, according to Sarah Bryner, a director who studies campaign finance at Public Agenda, a research organization focused on democracy.   "People from California really don't feel like they have much to do because their state's going to go blue regardless," she said. "So they support candidates in states like Georgia or Texas."   Democrats took the lead, but Republicans are catching up   While both parties now benefit from out-of-state funds, Democrats tended to rely on them, due to weaker local funding systems in competitive states like Ohio and Michigan. As a result, Democrats built a system for grassroots donations — ActBlue which launched in 2004 — nearly 15 years before Republicans, who launched WinRed in 2019.    
   While some of the Democratic advantage in out-of-state fundraising can be attributed to Republican incumbents' connections to local funding, part of it can be attributed to the Democratic Party's diverse base of voters.   "You're having to bring together that diverse coalition, not necessarily around some unified ideological agenda, but based on a kind of discrete policy [that] claims to represent particular groups," said Brandeis University's Zachary Albert.   Meanwhile, Republicans were initially slow to realize the potential for small dollar fundraising until Trump.   
   "The Republicans realized, especially during Trump, that they do have a national audience of small donors ready to activate behind their preferred candidates for their preferred agenda," Public Agenda's Sarah Bryner said.   Looking forward   While some states are trying to limit outside funds, like Hawaii implementing a cap on out-of-state donations starting in 2027, it's difficult to regulate at a national level, according to University of Massachusetts political science professor Raymond La Raja.   "It's going to be hard to do constitutionally, especially because the Supreme Court has ruled you can't prevent groups from spending as much money as they want in elections," he said.    
   In June, the Supreme Court ruled in favor of coordinated campaign spending which allows more out of state funds to be spent in elections. So far, the National Republican Senatorial Committee has spent three times as much on advertisements at this point than in the previous midterms.   La Raja suggested fund matching, where local donations would be matched with public funds, using New York City as a model. He believes this would shift candidates to focus more on their constituents' issues rather than national ones.   Bryner mentioned the Alaska top donor disclosure law as an option to localize fundraising. There, ads have to list the top three donors. Colorado and Virginia have similar laws for online and broadcast ads.   While funding can influence how a candidate talks about their race locally and nationally, Bryner isn't convinced this will completely tip the scale of elections. Candidates who've outraised with out-of-state funds, like Amy McGrath, who ran against Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell in Kentucky and Beto O'Rourke against Republican Sen. Ted Cruz in Texas, often lose against their opponents. She advises against appealing to donors out-of-state because ultimately it doesn't translate into votes.   "As much as money in politics is such a factor in America, voters are still ultimately who makes the final decision" Bryner said. "And if you're getting all your money from outside of the state, those people can't vote for you."

title: Minnesota becomes battleground as political clashes shape Senate race
description:
Minnesota becomes battleground as political clashes shape Senate race

body:
Minnesota becomes battleground as political clashes shape Senate race
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6019356/nx-s1-9981506" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Minnesota has become a flashpoint in the political dispute between President Trump and Democrats. Clashes over immigration and recent accusations of fraud are spilling into the U.S. Senate race.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:  The U.S. Senate race in Minnesota is especially competitive. It's an open seat. A Democrat is retiring. So while Democrats expect to gain Senate seats elsewhere in the country, Republicans hope to gain a seat in Minnesota. Democratic voters this year are motivated by immigration after a Trump administration crackdown led to protests and deaths in Minnesota. President Trump and the Republican Party are also focused on immigrants - in particular, Somali Americans and Representative Ilhan Omar. Minnesota Public Radio's Clay Masters reports.CLAY MASTERS, BYLINE: Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan sits in an elementary school library for a recent roundtable to talk about the local effects of President Trump's immigration enforcement.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PEGGY FLANAGAN: If folks just want to introduce yourself, and then just...MASTERS: Flanagan is the Democratic candidate for the open U.S. Senate race here. She says what happened in her state shows how the Trump administration wields its power, and it's what this midterm election is about.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)FLANAGAN: This is, I think, the model of what the most corrupt, cruel administration in our nation's history - what they can get away with when, you know, this goes unchecked. So this is a choice in this race.MASTERS: Flanagan faces Republican Michele Tafoya, who is running as a moderate and has the endorsement of President Trump. At a debate earlier this month hosted by Minnesota Public Radio, Tafoya was asked to comment on how Operation Metro Surge was handled. She brings up the two Americans who were killed by federal agents that sparked nationwide protests.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)MICHELE TAFOYA: Those two things go hand in hand. The loss of Renee Good and Alex Pretti is devastating. I did not like the way that ICE rollout was handled by Kristi Noem, and she was appropriately fired. We also had a massive failure in leadership from Governor Tim Walz and Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan.MASTERS: The Trump administration used both alleged and proven fraud in state social service programs as part of its reason for targeting Minnesota. And now voters are being flooded with ads tying hundreds of millions of dollars in alleged fraud to the state's Democratic leaders, including Minnesota's governor, Tim Walz, the party's former vice presidential candidate. That speaks to conservative voter Dale Johnson. He's a retired snowplow driver who says he brings the issue up at his union meetings, only to be met with pushback.DALE JOHNSON: And one of the fellow members said, oh, that was mostly federal money. As if, well, don't worry about it. It's federal money that they're blowing. That shows you that people aren't really using their head.MASTERS: In the final weeks before election day, President Trump continues to focus on Minnesota. Here he is in the Oval Office just last week, talking about a new program to report suspected fraud. And he used the opportunity to attack Minnesota and its Somali American community.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I remember Minnesota in the old days. What a beautiful - with lakes all over the place. They have more lakes than any place I've ever seen. So beautiful. They've - they're destroying it. Probably - maybe they've destroyed it.MASTERS: In that same appearance, Trump brought up the federal investigation into allegations of immigration fraud regarding Representative Ilhan Omar. The Minnesota congresswoman says it's an intimidation attempt ahead of the midterms. UC Berkeley law professor Ian Lopez studies the exploitation of race as a basis for mobilizing political support.IAN LOPEZ: These allegations of fraud against people of color in Minnesota as a way to whip up racial resentment and to try and transmute that into political energy - those are classic techniques of dogmas of politics.MASTERS: But immigration and fraud are among the issues Democrats and the Trump administration have been fighting over all year long, and the race for Minnesota's open U.S. Senate seat is closer than expected in a state that historically tilts blue.For NPR News, I'm Clay Masters in Minneapolis.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: How a lifelong Republican came to lead the data center battle in Ohio
description: Nick Owens, an attorney in Brown County,
body:
Nick Owens, an attorney in Brown County, Ohio, stands at the edge of a Mt. Orab neighborhood next to farmland that has been sold to a data center developer. Owens is leading an effort to halt the buildout of hyperscale data centers in communities like this one.
                
                    Andrea Hsu/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrea Hsu/NPR
    

   
   Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly.      MT. ORAB, Ohio — The data center mystery in this rural exurb of Cincinnati has consumed Nick Owens.   The lifelong Republican and self-described small-town attorney has spent countless hours trying to figure out what's going on with 1,000 acres of farmland and trees that property records show were sold to a data center developer in 2024 and 2025.   In a few spots, the data center property runs right up against beautiful two-story homes.   "This is the Ohio that people brag about. This is the Ohio people love. This is the small town charm," he says. "Living in the rural area, but getting the benefits of a nice, lovely neighborhood."   
   Some of the most coordinated opposition to data centers anywhere in the country grew out of what happened in secrecy in this village of 4,300 people, a short drive up a country road from Owens' home.   Nondisclosure agreements have stymied Owens' efforts to learn more. But along his quest, he crossed paths with another local attorney and a real estate agent who were equally alarmed. Together, they mobilized a network of volunteers in nearly all 88 counties in the state. They are Democrats, Republicans and Independents. They called themselves Conserve Ohio.   
   "We all share the same ethos and the same passion for preserving our way of life, preserving the future of Ohio, frankly, from the hyperscale data center invasion," says Owens. "It's really beautiful."   This fall, the group is behind ballot initiatives in 10 communities that would amend local charters to prohibit the construction of large-scale data centers — the kind used to power artificial intelligence. It's an effort that goes beyond the temporary pauses that hundreds of municipal and county governments have embraced.   "All too often you hear from the politicians, 'Well, the community should have a say,'" says Owens. "We're going to find out in ten communities whether or not the communities want them."   
   Meanwhile, the grassroots group is working on a more ambitious undertaking: a petition for an amendment to the state constitution that would ban large-scale data centers statewide. Their goal is to put that to Ohio's voters in 2027.   Data centers bring economic benefits and angst   It's been more than a decade since tech companies first came to Ohio, drawn by the state's inexpensive and abundant land, its energy infrastructure and its generous tax breaks. That combination paved the way for some of the fastest data center growth in the country.   Now, despite the economic benefits — considerable tax revenue, money for schools, numerous construction jobs and a smaller number of permanent jobs — no one seems to want a computing campus in their backyard, especially one shrouded in secrecy.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Signs opposing data centers outnumber campaign signs in a neighborhood in Mt. Orab, Ohio.
                
                    Andrea Hsu/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrea Hsu/NPR
    

   
   "Should the school have extra money or the local government have extra money so we have a constant hum and ridiculous amounts of emissions and pollution?" Owens says, pointing out that hyperscale data centers will require new power plants. "Our community is not for sale."   Pressed to consider whether the state should forgo all opportunities, Owens says he'd entertain the idea of putting data centers on old industrial sites, where they'd be buffered from people.   "If we're going to have data centers, those are the prime places," he says, while acknowledging that it'd be cheaper and easier for a developer to build on pristine farmland than on an old coal site. "I don't know if there are enough brownfield sites, but shouldn't we start with those first?"   A hot-button election issue   In recent months, candidates running for statewide office in Ohio have been trying to convince voters that they hear their concerns — even as they stop short of backing the kind of sweeping moratorium data center opponents are seeking.   Conserve Ohio has not endorsed any of them.   
   Until recently, data center projects weren't all that controversial, in part because they were smaller and weren't being built for AI.   But as the issue has gained traction, it's become a hot topic in the midterms, including in the tight race to fill a U.S. Senate seat. Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown has cast his opponent, the incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, as "the face of data centers." Brown has been reminding voters that as lieutenant governor, Husted welcomed tech companies to Ohio and championed their data center investments.   
   Meanwhile, Husted has accused Brown of hypocrisy, pointing to Brown's past support for data centers.   Husted has also introduced his own solution, pushing a bill in Congress aimed at getting data centers to pay for power grid upgrades and other costs associated with their massive energy use. Senate Democrats have blocked the bill, calling it toothless, prompting Husted to accuse the Democrats of not caring or helping.   Unconvinced that politicians will help   These political gestures have not persuaded Linda Moodie, an independent who's been volunteering with Conserve Ohio. She doesn't trust that any of the candidates running for statewide office "will do the right thing" if elected, which is to give the people a say in the data center buildout.   "It's really something that I think a lot of us didn't see coming, and all of a sudden there's just an influx of them," she says.   While Moodie wonders if all the talk on the campaign trail is simply to get votes, she says she will cast her ballot for Brown, who she thinks has been talking about data centers the longest.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Linda Moodie (right), a volunteer with Conserve Ohio, collects signatures for a petition to ban large-scale data centers statewide at a Halloween event in Fairfield, Ohio, on Oct. 22, 2026.
                
                    Andrea Hsu/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrea Hsu/NPR
    

   
   And meanwhile, between now and election day, she's seizing every opportunity to collect signatures to get the statewide ban on the ballot next year.   On a recent evening, she set up a booth at the "Halloween on the Green" celebration in the Cincinnati suburb of Fairfield. She handed out candy to kids and clipboards with the petition to parents. Both were enthusiastically received.   
   "The closer it hits to home, the more people that are going to want to do something," says Moodie.   A dampening of voter enthusiasm in a Republican stronghold   Two years ago, Owens served as a Trump delegate at the Republican National Convention. He won't say how he's voting this fall, but he says no doubt the data center issue, along with $6 diesel, have dampened Republican enthusiasm.   Throughout Mt. Orab, the absence of campaign yard signs is notable.   "Two years ago you would have seen Donald Trump signs left and right," says Owens.   This county, like much of rural Ohio, voted 80% for President Trump in 2024.   
   "You always have depressed votes in the midterms," says Owens. "But I think the enthusiasm gap for Republicans in particularly rural areas is going to be a lot more pronounced… than any type of enthusiasm gap for Democrats in the cities."   Trump's belittling of data center opponents isn't helping, he says, citing recent comments the president posted to his social media platform Truth Social.   "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," Trump wrote. "If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame."   Owens calls the president's statements "tone deaf."   "I mean, no one wants to be poor or backwards," he says. "I want our regular way of life."   Construction at the Mt. Orab site hasn't yet begun. It's not clear when it will. Owens says because of nondisclosure agreements, people who live here know nothing.   For now, standing at the edge of the data center property on a crisp fall day, it's nearly silent but for the birds.

title: A breakthrough for the group on the trail of Chinese hackers
description:
Chinese government hackers are secretly burrowing into critical networks using creative new methods.   

    
        
          Transcript
body:
Chinese government hackers are secretly burrowing into critical networks using creative new methods.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  Chinese government hackers have spent the last several years quietly burrowing into critical networks using novel tactics to try and stay hidden. However, some cybersecurity researchers have been able to stay on their tails. NPR's Jenna McLaughlin has the story.JENNA MCLAUGHLIN, BYLINE: Michael Horka has been watching network traffic flowing along the backbone of the internet for years.MICHAEL HORKA: I'm a principal information security analyst at Lumen's Black Lotus Labs. We identify, track and disrupt nation state and criminal threat actors as they traverse the internet.MCLAUGHLIN: Lumen is a major telecommunications company that helps route network traffic. While hackers can cover some tracks, they can't fully hide all their digital footprints. But they sure are trying.HORKA: It definitely felt like a wild goose chase a lot of times.MCLAUGHLIN: That leads us to Volt Typhoon, a Chinese government hacking group that U.S. national security officials have said is focused on secretly getting access to key strategic targets.HORKA: Heavy in the government and defense sector, telecommunications, broad communications in general, critical infrastructure. We've got water, rail, aviation.MCLAUGHLIN: Officials say those targets aren't by accident. They're great for intelligence gathering, but adversaries could also cause physical damage, like shut off the power or cut off access to ports, for example, creating societal panic or preventing the U.S. military from responding quickly in the event of a conflict. It's been a focus for years. That hasn't changed, but they've gotten a lot sneakier, Horka says. These hackers have created a roadmap for accessing critical networks that Horka's team at Black Lotus is calling Silent Train.HORKA: It was a lot of thread pulling, but as we pulled on those threads, we eventually made it back to somewhat of a reproducible pattern - a reproducible network pattern that we were able to signature.MCLAUGHLIN: In other words, these hackers would create a new winding pathway through up to six different virtual networks and compromised devices like routers to get to their ultimate destination every single time, never retracing their steps. Meanwhile, they used previously undiscovered vulnerabilities and covered their tracks behind them.HORKA: They were purposely trying to stay extremely quiet.MCLAUGHLIN: Beyond the novel spy tactics, there's a larger message Horka wants to send - that these hackers are highly motivated and willing to invest in these operations. Defenders need to do the same.HORKA: It's important for network defenders and threat hunters to put on that black hat for a moment and just think, like, hey, if this is really valuable to us as an organization, it would probably be a target as well.MCLAUGHLIN: Horka hopes that exposing Volt Typhoon's trade craft might at least make it harder for them to hide.HORKA: If I had to use an analogy, if the pond water has just been sitting for so long and nothing's happening, and there's nothing you can do, like, we're dropping a rock in it, and we're going to see what happens.MCLAUGHLIN: Horka will be watching to see the ripples.Jenna McLaughlin, NPR News.(SOUNDBITE OF REFUGEE CAMP ALL-STARS SONG, "THE SWEETEST THING (FEAT LAURYN HILL)")

title: Hackers expose the identities of more than 40,000 DHS employees
description: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security
body:
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security emblem on the U.S.Immigration and Customs Enforcement building as seen on January 07, 2026 in Washington, D.C.
                
                    Heather Diehl/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Heather Diehl/Getty Images North America
    

   
   A hacking group cracked the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's personnel files, exposing the names, phone numbers and addresses of more than 40,000 DHS agents, operatives, and associates, on Wednesday, including those involved in undercover operations.   "On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat.' This is what happens to ICE when you do that," a spokesperson for the hacktivist group behind the breach, the Department of Peace, said in an online statement.   The hackers said they stole the data by subverting DHS's single sign on system, according to an online post. It said it distributed that material to the group Distributed Denial of Secrets, which posted it online in a database called Icepick. The Department of Peace also shared the trove of data with Ryan Ottignon, a U.S.-based journalist, and a Swiss hacker known as maia arson crimew. Together, the two created a searchable online database, with crimew doing all of the technical work, Ottignon told NPR.   
   DDoSecrets cofounder Emma Best called the leak "extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity," because it makes explicit connections between "officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations …along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs."   Other activists say the information will be a boon to those investigating DHS and filing freedom of information requests, which, due to a lack of specific information, like names, email addresses, can often yield useless results.   In a statement, DHS said it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The department added that it is taking necessary steps to "ensure all are properly protected."   More than 21,000 records identify employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Another 10,000 relate to Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees and its Homeland Security Investigations unit.   It is an unprecedented breach of intelligence, coming on the heels of similar hacking attacks at the FBI. However, the database is far from comprehensive and represents about a fifth of Homeland Security's workforce, which staffs a little more than 220,000 people.   Ottignon, who has worked on similar data leak projects in the past, rejected suggestions that he and others connected to the Department of Peace or Distribution Denials of Secrets were doxing government employees.   
   "We are in a situation in which a group of public officials go around into cities and states and all around the country, and they seek to hide who they are. Very frequently using masks, wearing plain clothes. And they do universally unspeakable things to these communities," Ottignon said. He added that he believed that kind of behavior is unacceptable in a free society.   "We need oversight for useful government, if it exists at all. So this is just one step in that oversight process," he added.   In a note attached to the files, DDoSecrets wrote, "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs."

title: Judge denies the Justice Department's bid to stop processing California ballots
description: People extract ballots from their envelo
body:
People extract ballots from their envelopes and prepare them to be scanned for counting in the Vote-By-Mail Processing Boards area at the Orange County Registrar of Voters Facility in Santa Ana, Calif., on Oct. 28.
                
                    Apu Gomes/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Apu Gomes/Getty Images
    

   
   A federal judge has denied an unprecedented, emergency request by the Department of Justice to segregate thousands of California ballots in the midterm elections.   The Justice Department wants California election officials to stop processing ballots pertaining to 20,000 individuals that federal officials say are "likely" noncitizens.   
   State and local officials in California have countered that the DOJ's list of "likely" noncitizens is unreliable, with a preliminary analysis by Los Angeles County showing that many on the list do not have active voter registrations. The officials also claim that setting aside ballots just days before Election Day, when voting and processing mailed ballots are already underway, would be unlawful and infeasible and would disenfranchise eligible voters.   In his 26-page ruling issued Wednesday evening, U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton appointee, denied the Justice Department's request for a temporary restraining order to stop processing the ballots in question.   
   "Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," he wrote.   Carter also expressed concern about taking action that could disenfranchise eligible voters and create chaos.   "Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred," Carter wrote at the conclusion of his order. "If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process."   
   The judge said that the federal government can address the issue by continuing to indict people for the crime of illegally voting as noncitizens. DOJ officials say in the last two months they have charged dozens of people for registering or voting without being a U.S. citizen.   The DOJ's lawsuit in California, which was filed Oct. 15, is among a flurry of unprecedented actions the department has waged in states close to Election Day, raising alarms about federal interference in state election procedures.   Like in California, on Monday federal prosecutors asked Washington state election officials to review a list of 400 registered voters the DOJ believes are likely noncitizens. And last week, the DOJ filed an unusual lawsuit in Alaska that seeks to stop the state from certifying the results in its Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses due to votes for a longshot candidate with a similar name who is accused of being a spoiler candidate.   
   In California's most recent motion to the court, state Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, asked the judge to take into account the circumstances of DOJ's demand. "This litigation is a precursor to further interference here in California," Bonta wrote. "The Court must not be drawn into this chilling degradation of democratic values and constitutional principles."   The Department of Justice quickly filed a notice that it is appealing Carter's denial. The matter could ultimately wind up before the U.S. Supreme Court.   "Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution," Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, wrote on X, adding that he would be seeking an emergency order from the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.    The DOJ has argued the issue is urgent since once signatures are verified on returned mail ballot envelopes, the ballots are separated from their envelopes to retain voter confidentiality, making it impossible to retrieve an ineligible ballot.    Voting by noncitizens has been shown by audits and investigations to be extremely rare.   "Tonight's decision makes clear that the federal government's actions are election interference," said Jonathan Miller, chief program officer at Public Rights Project, which is counsel for Los Angeles County.   "The district court unequivocally found that DOJ's claims are unsubstantiated, that it has no basis to bring its lawsuit, and it has presented no evidence to justify its actions. The administration claims to be protecting election integrity while, at every turn, undermining the systems and federal support that safeguard our elections," Miller said.   Bonta, California's attorney general, said in a statement the ruling is an important victory, "But this fight is not over. We will keep fighting to protect California's elections from unlawful federal interference and get this baseless lawsuit dismissed."   The accuracy of the DOJ's list of "likely" noncitizens is still an ongoing matter of dispute.   
   A Los Angeles County analysis of a small sample of people on the DOJ's list found that a significant portion had said in records they were born in the U.S. But U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services senior official Nicolas Bartell contested that in recent court filings, writing that his office's review of those individuals found none were U.S.-born.   Bartell did acknowledge the review found four of those people "might have a claim to U.S. citizenship."   He also provided the court additional details about the federal government's methodology in creating the list in recent court filings.   But University of Delaware political scientist Kassra Oskooi, who has been tapped as an expert witness by voting rights groups who are intervening in the case, responded in his own declaration to the court that he believes USCIS's matching protocol "is likely to be unreliable."   Carter wrote in his order the federal government's protocol "raises significant concerns" and that he could not conclude its process is credible.

title: Why many student voters have a right to choose where to register to vote
description: Students at the University of Virginia h
body:
Students at the University of Virginia help eligible voters register to vote in Charlottesville, Va., in 2024.
                
                    Ryan M. Kelly/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Ryan M. Kelly/AP
    

   
   Many student voters studying outside their hometown face a key decision before they even get a ballot: Should they register to vote where they go to school?   A Supreme Court ruling in 1979 affirmed the right of eligible students to register in the communities where they live during the academic year. But close to a half-century later, some people continue to question why students can vote in their college towns.   That issue resurfaced in discussions about changes Montana made last year to its requirements for residents who want to register to vote. After a student advocacy group sued, a state judge blocked the new restriction for now. That leaves the previous rules in place for Montana students who want to register to vote, including for the midterm elections through Election Day.   
   Now, as the wait continues for the judge's final ruling, some experts on student voting see the case as a reminder of common misunderstandings about the rights of some of the country's youngest voters.   Why out-of-state college students are like owners of multiple homes   Voting in the U.S. is tied to residency, and state and local governments determine who qualifies as a resident who can register.   To make sure certain voters, such as eligible students, are not discriminated against, federal law sets ground rules for residency requirements, explains Michael Hanmer, a professor of government and politics at the University of Maryland, whose research has focused on student voters.   "You can't apply different standards to different groups of people, so college students need to be treated the same as anybody else in the mix here who might be new to a particular place," Hanmer says.   
   All eligible voters have a right to cast a ballot somewhere. And like owners of multiple homes, many students are able to choose which of their residences to be that somewhere for registering to vote. In the legal world, it's known as their "domicile."   "It's defined as the one singular, fixed, permanent, principal home where one intends to return, although she may not currently reside there," explains Yael Bromberg, an attorney who co-edited the book Youth Voting Rights: Civil Rights, the Twenty-Sixth Amendment, and the Fight for American Democracy on College Campuses. "In the case of a student who may not know where she might live after graduation, that determination of domicile is highly personal and an individualized assessment."   
   How Montana's new law could stop thousands of eligible students from voting   In Montana, a U.S. citizen who is 18 or older and has been a state resident for at least 30 days is generally eligible to register to vote there.   Last year, Montana's Republican-controlled legislature passed a new restriction for "temporary" residents in an "educational program." Under the revised state law, they could only register in a Montana county if they intend to make the county or the state their permanent home at the end of their program.   GOP state officials argue that restriction does not apply to students at colleges and universities in Montana. That interpretation, they claim in a court filing, "would render the word 'temporary' meaningless, because no one understands obtaining a two, four, or eight-year degree as a temporary endeavor."   So far, Missoula County Judge Jason Marks is not buying that argument. In February, he found the restriction against student voters likely violates Montana's constitution.   After holding a hearing this month, Marks is now preparing his final ruling for the lawsuit brought by student advocates at the Montana Public Interest Research Group. MontPIRG claims the change to Montana's residency rule could force thousands of students to lose the ability to have a say at the ballot box about how their communities are run.   Why out-of-state student voters should be aware of other state requirements   At a public hearing last year, some of the restriction's supporters said student voters from outside Montana should not be able to affect the state's elections.   But Hanmer at the University of Maryland doesn't see Montana's law clearing legal hurdles.   "I would be surprised if this attempt to restrict students from voting if they're in Montana just for educational purposes holds up," he says.   Still, Hanmer points out student voters who do have the right to choose where to register should keep in mind that, in some states, that choice may come with other requirements.   
   "If they want to follow through and vote in that new state, then they might have to engage in some additional activities that could be costly in terms of their time," Hanmer says. Certain states require a new resident to, for example, get a new state ID or change their car registration. "They can impose these restrictions," Hanmer adds, "but they impose them on all new residents, not just college students."   Edited by Benjamin Swasey

title: Israel's election too close to call. And, the Ebola outbreak reaches grim milestone
description:
Trump Rallies For Republicans, Israel Election Results, Fed Interest Rates Meeting
    
            
                
                Tr
body:
Trump Rallies For Republicans, Israel Election Results, Fed Interest Rates Meeting
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-150313/nx-s1-mx-6020166-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Midterm ad spending has surpassed a record $11 billion, according to Ad Impact. An NPR analysis found that candidates in four major Senate races spent more than $15 million on fundraising ads in the 2025-26 election cycle. Meanwhile, President Trump has been campaigning in tight races across states like Texas, Mississippi, and Kansas.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaks during a campaign event on October 17, 2026 in Marietta, Georgia.
                
                    Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 Trump has not been sticking with his standard midterm pitch, which includes touting GOP tax cuts and attacking Democrats, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben tells Up First. His jokes, including comments about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted's physique, entertain rally crowds but distract from the key issues the median voter cares about, like the economy and gas prices. Midterm turnout is usually low, but the GOP base still supports him, suggesting many MAGA votes are available, Kurtzleben says. But Trump needing to rally votes in very red states indicates a potential problem for his party.   The election in Israel is too close to call after voters turned out in record numbers to decide whether to keep Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in office or oust him for an alternative. Netanyahu was in a tight race with his top rival Gadi Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief of staff. Final vote tallies may take time, and if no bloc secures a majority, it could take days or weeks for party leaders to form a governing coalition and determine the next prime minister.   
   🎧 Israelis went to bed thinking Eisenkot had the advantage, but by morning, Netanyahu pulled ahead, making the election too close to call, NPR's Daniel Estrin says. Election officials tell NPR that they expect to finish counting votes by tomorrow afternoon. The leading candidate will have six weeks to form a governing coalition, likely competing for support from defectors in each other's camps. Eisenkot could gain the majority of lawmakers' support in parliament, thanks to a strong showing from Arab-led parties eager to see him as prime minister. Eisenkot's camp is hesitant to form a coalition with Arab parties due to mistrust and demonization of Arab political leaders after the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, Estrin says. He adds that both candidates don't have a clear path to a majority coalition.   The Federal Reserve typically combats inflation by raising interest rates. While prices are currently rising faster than average wages, investors don't expect a rate hike at today's meeting.   🎧 The Labor Department's latest cost-of-living report shows consumer prices rose 3.7% in September compared to last year. NPR's Scott Horsley says that marks a larger annual increase than the previous month. Fed policymakers raised interest rates in September, but investors believe the central bank will remain low-key ahead of Election Day and may increase rates again in December.   
   The Ebola outbreak has surpassed 10,000 people infected since its declaration in May, according to the latest figures from the Democratic Republic of Congo. This outbreak has spread faster than any in history. It is also the largest in geographic scope, spanning from Nigeria to Kenya, and is second in death toll with nearly 5,000 deaths. Around one-third of those who have died have been children.   On the ground   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        NPR
    

   
   The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.   With Election Day less than a week away, Morning Edition's Michel Martin went to the Midwest to hear from voters about what is important to them this midterm cycle. In Springfield, Ohio, the Trump administration has conducted an aggressive campaign to deport Haitian residents who have been living legally in the country with Temporary Protected Status. The administration revoked TPS for Haitians during Trump's second term. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed has narrowly won the Democratic Senate nomination, a victory for the party's progressive wing. The swing state is important to both parties, which is why Trump and former President Barack Obama campaigned for their party's Senate candidate over the weekend.   Hear what voters in these two states had to say:   🎧 In Michigan, many voters expressed burnout as they worry about gas prices and healthcare.🎧 Trump's tariffs are hitting Michigan households harder than any other state because many people depend on cross-border trade. But voters affected said the issue isn't so clear-cut.🎧 Winning a statewide office in Michigan without Detroit is challenging, and El-Sayed didn't perform well there in the primary. Some Black Detroiters said they remain skeptical of him.🎧 Some Springfield, Ohio voters said they are voting early because they are angry about the administration's treatment of Haitians.   
   Follow the reporting on Morning Edition, NPR.org, in the NPR app and in this newsletter.   The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.   Life advice   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                To free up more time in your life, writer Caroline Sylge proposes a creative idea: Give yourself a "say no" retreat. It's a day to look at your calendar and thoughtfully decline obligations in the next few weeks and months.
                
                    Juan Moyano/ Moment RF/ Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Juan Moyano/ Moment RF/ Getty Images
    

   
   As the holidays approach and appointments and commitments begin to pile up, author Caroline Sylge recommends a "say no" retreat — a day dedicated to figuring out which obligations you want to decline in the coming weeks and months. While it may seem unconventional to devote an entire day to saying no, this approach can help create space for what truly matters to you. Sylge shared with Life Kit her suggested schedule for a "say no" retreat:   🙅 As soon as you wake up, list things you want to say no to. Identify the obvious tasks you want to avoid.🙅 Take a break, then return to your retreat space and expand your "say no" list. Review requests, appointments, volunteer work and commitments for the coming days, weeks and months. Note the tasks you want to decline, and why.🙅 After another break, review your list and start saying no. Start with a small win, like crossing off a demanding task. Next, focus on the tougher rejections that may involve saying no to someone you care about or work with.   For more guidance on a "say no" retreat, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Dalia Luque, left, has her face painted by Amber Lovold, one of the organizers of a midnight release party at Politics and Prose in Washington, D.C. They are celebrating the publication of A Court of Splintered Harmony, the latest installment of Sarah J. Maas' popular romantasy series.
                
                    Ella Mitchell/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Ella Mitchell/NPR
    

   
   The latest installment of Sarah J. Maas' A Court of Thorns and Roses came out on Tuesday, prompting thousands of fans to attend midnight release parties at bookstores nationwide.A federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration's plans to further change East Potomac Park, the municipal D.C. golf course that the president wants to turn into a championship-level venue.Harvard astrophysicists have found what they believe is a previously undiscovered dwarf planet in our solar system. (via WGBH)

title: A judge halted D.C. golf course renovations. Trump says they'll still start next month
description: President Trump, seen touring the East P
body:
President Trump, seen touring the East Potomac Golf Links in late June, says his administration will appeal the judge's ruling and close the course for renovations next month.
                
                    Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   After weeks of tense hearings and late-night court filings, a federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from making any further alterations to East Potomac Park, the municipal D.C. golf course that the president wants to redevelop into a championship-level venue.   The long-simmering legal battle kicked into high gear in recent weeks, after the government cut down 430 trees on the golf course with less than a day's notice. That prompted a pair of lengthy court hearings that at times turned heated, with government officials repeatedly insisting that the tree-clearing was unrelated to the renovations President Trump had touted on social media. They contradicted the president's own social media posts from that very morning by saying there was no final plan for those renovations at all.   
   "Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting president," U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote in her 70-page opinion. "And yet, here we are."   
   Reyes extended what was initially a two-week halt to tree removal, ordering the government not to cut down "or substantially prune or otherwise damage or impair" any trees at East Potomac Park without a court order. She also ordered it to provide "no less than ten business days' written advance notice" before closing or making any "irreversible modification" to any parts of the park while the legal battle plays out.   "By issuing this preliminary injunction, the Court does not end the round: it simply marks the ball until the parties can fully and fairly litigate this case," Reyes wrote.   Monday's ruling is a win for the D.C. Preservation League and a pair of local golfers who sued to prevent renovations earlier this year — and for the growing grassroots movement to protect the municipal course and the surrounding recreational area, which is beloved by runners, cyclists, birders and others.   "We are grateful the court intervened to stop the Trump-Vance administration's greed and lawlessness while the case continues, and we are eager to argue the case in court," said Skye Perryman, the president of the nonprofit Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs.   
   In a Truth Social post late Monday, Trump said the Department of the Interior will appeal the ruling. NPR has reached out to the Department of Interior but did not hear back in time for publication.   Trump also doubled down on his earlier announcement that construction will begin on Nov. 15 and keep the park closed for 15 months, adding that the "judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project."   "To have to give advanced notices to a judge who has no expertise in Golf, Architecture, Landscaping, Construction, or anything else having to do with building such a World Class Project, is not fair, appropriate, or Constitutional," Trump wrote.   Reyes herself has said she is not interested in policing the federal government's landscaping efforts.   That's why, as she explained in Monday's opinion, she repeatedly declined to intervene in the case — instead issuing repeated warnings against any unannounced major alterations — until "the Government did what it assured all it would not do."   "The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" Reyes concluded. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."   On Tuesday afternoon, Reyes made a record of Trump's post and gave the government about 24 hours to clarify whether a plan exists to close East Potomac in mid-November and, if so, "how that can be reconciled" with what its lawyers previously told the court. She said she will schedule a status hearing for either Friday or Monday.    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A golfer plays near some of the 430 trees that were cut down at East Potomac earlier this month.
                
                    Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   The judge took aim at the government's contradictions   Reyes' strongly-worded 70-page opinion came exactly a week after a seven-hour hearing in which she clashed repeatedly with the government's lawyers. She had already rejected the administration's request to recuse herself from the case because of alleged bias.   
   Last week's hearing featured sworn testimony from several officials from the Department of the Interior and National Park Service, to provide a fuller account of the origins and purpose of the controversial tree-clearing. But it teed up bigger questions about whether the administration had misled the court and the public over its intentions for the golf course.   "This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more," Reyes wrote on Monday. "It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys."   
   Much of Reyes' opinion examines the gap between what Trump has said publicly and what his administration has told the court.   The most notable: Trump posted online the morning of last week's hearing that work would begin on the golf course "immediately." But hours later, in the courtroom, administration officials said in sworn testimony that they were not aware of any final plan.   Weaving together timelines and testimonies, Reyes ultimately agreed with plaintiffs that there does seem to be a golf course renovation plan (they refer to it as the "Washington National Plan") despite the administration's repeated denials.   "To be sure, the Court cannot pinpoint the exact date at which the Plan became final," Reyes wrote. "But it determines without hesitation that it occurred at some point well before October 15, 2026."   
   She doesn't accept the government's explanation that it cleared hundreds of healthy, non-invasive trees on such short notice to enact vegetation recommendations from a 2019 National Park Service Report (whose other recommendations, including for the city's other two municipal golf courses, went largely unaddressed in the last seven years). She called that justification "pretextual."   She took particular aim at the credibility of one witness, Gregory Wischer — a deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department — who was photographed carrying rolled-up concept plans while accompanying Trump and golf course architect Tom Fazio on a tour of East Potomac in June.   
   "Yet Wischer maintains that he — as Deputy Chief of Staff to the Secretary of the Interior — just spontaneously became interested in tree and vegetation management. In mid September. At the East Potomac Golf Course," Reyes wrote.   Reyes said the government "has made no compelling factual rebuttal." At one point, the administration accused the plaintiffs of conjecture "based on a handful of tweets." Reyes shut that down in Monday's opinion.   "The 'handful of tweets' are not complaints about the Red Sox's latest blown lead in the ninth. They are statements from the President of the United States, and from the Secretary of the Interior, about actions within their purview," she wrote. "And the posts say, in no uncertain terms, that a plan exists and that construction will start imminently — one even contains a final schematic of the Course's redesign."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                East Potomac Park, seen from the observation deck of the Washington Monument in July. The manmade peninsula is home to a municipal golf course and recreational areas, including a 3-mile road around the perimeter.
                
                    Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   What's next for East Potomac?    Trump said as recently as Monday night that he believes the renovations do not require approval. But, as Reyes pointed out in her opinion, administration officials acknowledged in a July hearing that major renovations would require federal environmental and historic preservation reviews.   Last week, however, administration lawyers presented an "alternative argument" that the renovations actually cannot be reviewed under the Administrative Procedure Act.   
   "It says, Emily Litella-style: 'Never mind,'" Reyes wrote, referring to the perpetually about-facing Saturday Night Live character. "But parties cannot change course whenever and however the evidence suits them … And so the Court does not credit this new argument."   Plaintiffs in the lawsuit argue that the government is purposefully approaching the golf course renovations as smaller projects — like dumping debris from the White House East Wing demolition last year or cutting down hundreds of trees this month — to avoid federally required environmental reviews.   That argument seems to hold water with Reyes, who said, the Interior Department likely violated the National Environmental Protection Act "by impermissibly segmenting its review of the Plan's environmental effects."   
   Monday's ruling — and the administration's promised appeal — could slow that process even more. Trump said on social media that work "must begin, immediately, if it is to be completed in a timely and seasonal manner."   But there are still many questions about the final product.   
   The rendering Trump shared earlier this month shows the park's three courses of varying ability levels combined into one that overtakes the entire peninsula, seemingly removing the perimeter road that runners and bikers use every day and raising questions about whether the historically affordable golf course could soon be less accessible.   Trump said Monday the redeveloped course will be able to host events like the PGA Championship and Ryder Cup, but will also be "open to the Public, at a reduced rate for those living in Washington, D.C."   The project is one of many ways he's looking to make his mark on the nation's capital, from building the White House ballroom to adding his name to the Kennedy Center to pushing through plans for a triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

schema.headline: A judge halted D.C. golf course renovations. Trump says they'll still start next month
